CallerKind.description: Who calls: the admin of the deployment, or a user of a tenant.
CallerKind.title: CallerKind

Condition.description:
One question about one field.

`value` is required: a condition without a value is not a condition, and a `None` default
let `Condition(field="name")` build happily, meaning "name equals nothing".

It is `JsonValue` and not `Any`: what a condition compares is a value that travelled in a
JSON — a number, a text, a boolean, a list of them — and `Any` let any Python object
through until the SQL translator tripped over it, far from here.

`operator` does have a default, and that is a different case: omitting it means equality.

Beside JSON it takes `datetime`, `date` and `Decimal`, because a Feature also builds
conditions from Python and forcing it to serialise a date to text for the model to read
back was a detour. In `model_dump(mode="json")` they come out as text all the same.
Condition.title: Condition

Count.description:
How many exist in total.

`exact=False` means *at least* `value`: counting stops at a ceiling so its cost does not
grow with the table. A client renders that as `10000+`, and a collection reads it as
"you are holding a fragment".
Count.title: Count

grouping.description:
How to split the result set, when it is being counted rather than listed. Ignored by a
plain search: a page of records has no buckets.

pagination.description: How many, and from where. Always the object: `{"limit": 80, "strategy": {"token": "eyJ…"}}`.

selection.description:
The filter: a `Condition`, or an `All`/`Any`/`Not` grouping more of them.

**The declared type is exactly what is accepted.** No abbreviated spelling and no
conversion, so pydantic and the type checker see the same thing and `criteria.selection` reads
with an exhaustive `match`. All the validator does is build the nodes when the tree
arrives serialised from JSON — which is the same tree, not another form.
selection.title: Selection

specification.description:
What to bring back of each record: field name → how to bring it, the value being a
criteria exactly like this one. `None` and `{}` are NOT the same thing:

    None    nothing was asked          →  every scalar, no relation expanded
    {}      asked, nothing survived    →  the identity alone

Read as one, a mask whose every field was dropped hands back the whole record, which is
exactly what it existed to prevent.

Cursor.description:
Locating a page by where the previous one ended. **The strategy this engine implements.**

    in      Cursor()                          the first page; nothing came before it
    in      Cursor(token="eyJrIjo…")          the next one, resumed from that row
    out     the rows past that row, in the criteria's own order

A row inserted or deleted mid-walk changes nothing, because the cursor names a ROW and not
a position. The token is minted from the last row of the page before; `keys_for` turns it
back into the keys it holds, checked against the ordering in play.
Cursor.title: Cursor

DraftState.description:
The record was answered from its owner's draft — what a form saved as a draft and
nobody stored yet.

`version` is what the next edit names as `version`; `stale` says the stored record moved on
since the draft started, so saving it would be refused.
DraftState.title: DraftState

Dropped.description:
A condition that was asked for and could not be honoured.

Reported rather than raised: a shared link outlives the schema it was written against, and
a dropped filter always *widens* the result — so it is dropped and said out loud.
Dropped.title: Dropped

EditAction.description:
What an `Edit` does with the record the form holds — save it as a draft, store it, or
drop it.
EditAction.title: EditAction

FieldState.description: How a form shows one field for the record a preview built: its hints, evaluated.

items.description:
For a list of records — an invoice's lines —, how a form shows each one's fields, by the
record: its identity, or its position for a record that has none (`"2"`). Empty for any
other field, for a relation nobody read and for the records a many-to-many references.
items.title: Items

FieldState.title: FieldState

FormWarning.description:
A warning to a form about the values it holds; it refuses nothing.

FormWarning(message="a discount above 10% needs approval", field="discount", path=("discount",))
FormWarning(message="price below cost", field="lines", path=("lines", 2, "price"))

`path` is where it points inside the record — a line's cell included, by its position in the
list the form sent — and `field` the record's own field it is under (`path[0]`); both empty
when the warning is about the record as a whole.

blocks_save.description:
Whether saving the record as it is would be refused: an `@check` that fails here fails the
save; `warn_form` only advises.
blocks_save.title: Blocks Save

rule.description:
The rule that warned (`Sale.delivery_when_confirmed`), when an `@check` did; `None` for
advice the domain gave with `warn_form`.
rule.title: Rule

FormWarning.title: FormWarning

FromContext.description:
A value of the server's own context — the user, the tenant, a date it holds — never one the
client sends.

key.description: The key it reads, as the context holds it.
key.title: Key

plus.description: How far to move it, signed: `{"days": -30}` is thirty days ago.

start_of.description: The start of the calendar unit it falls in once moved: `month` is the first of the month.

FromContext.title: FromContext

FromField.description:
Another field of the same row: a column compared with a column.

    {"field": "total", "operator": ">", "value": {"$": "field", "name": "credit_limit"}}

It is not read before the row: it is the other side of the comparison, and it takes only the
operators that compare (`=`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`) and a field of the same type.

name.description: The field it reads, of the same entity.
name.title: Name

FromField.title: FromField

Grain.description: A calendar unit a date snaps to the start of.
Grain.title: Grain

Grouping.description:
How a result set is split: the levels, and the numbers folded out of every group.

    in      {"by": ["produced_by", "registered_at:month"], "measures": {"filas": ["sum", "row_count"]}}
    out     every level `by` names, each group counted and folded, carrying how to open it

All the levels named are answered, one statement each: grouping by three fields is three
statements whatever the number of rows. A screen that drills down one click at a time asks
for one level and, on the click, reads `bucket.criteria` with a grouping of its own; it never
has to know how deep the whole tree is.

group_by.description: The levels the set is split by, one statement each.
group_by.title: Group By

measures.description: The numbers every group answers, each under a name the caller chose.
measures.title: Measures

order.description:
How the groups of each level come back: by the level's own field, by a name in `measures`
or by `count`. Empty means by the level's field, ascending, which is how a list of groups
reads when nobody asked for anything else. It orders the GROUPS; `Criteria.order` orders
the rows, and with a page asked for it decides which rows each group shows first.
order.title: Order

pagination.description:
How many groups of the FIRST level come back, and from where. `None`, the default, is
every group: a grouping is a set of counts and a client asked for all of them. When a page
is asked, the deeper levels answer only for the groups that survived it.

A page and not a keyset: ordering by an aggregate has no stable key to resume from, so
`Offset` is the honest strategy here and a cursor is not minted.

where_measures.description:
A filter over what the groups measured, not over the rows: `count > 10`, `debit > 1000`.

The names it may use are the ones in `measures` plus `count`. `where` filters the rows that
make the groups; this filters the groups those rows made — which is why it is not called
`where`: it reads measures, not fields.
where_measures.title: Where Measures

Grouping.title: Grouping

GroupingLevel.description:
One level of grouping: the field it splits by, and how.

in      "produced_by"           →  GroupingLevel(field='produced_by')
in      "registered_at:month"   →  GroupingLevel(field='registered_at', grain=Grain.MONTH)
in      {"field": "registered_at", "part": "month"}   →  every March, whatever the year

A **grain** cuts a date into ranges of time (`2026-03`); a **part** extracts a number from it
(`3`). One level takes one or the other, never both.

`fill` lists every value the level can take, including the ones with no rows, as groups with
a count of 0: all the choices of an enum, both values of a boolean, every number a part can
be, every grain of a date range that `where` bounds. An axis that is complete is what a chart
needs, and what a group that happened to be empty would otherwise silently leave out.
GroupingLevel.title: GroupingLevel

Measure.description:
One number a group answers: a function over a field, under a name the caller chose.

    in      {"function": "sum", "field": "row_count"}
    out     Measure(function='sum', field='row_count')       → sum(row_count) AS <name>

**Named parts and not `"sum:row_count"`**, so nobody has to split a string in whatever
language is reading this — the same reason a condition travels as `{field, operator,
value}`. The pair `["sum", "row_count"]` is read as well, because writing one by hand in
Python is a pair; what a caller sends over a wire is the object.

It is called a measure and not an aggregate on purpose: in this codebase an *aggregate* is
the DDD root — what `Meta.aggregate` names — and two meanings for one word in the same
sentence is how a reader loses an afternoon.

argument.description:
What the function needs besides a column, when it needs anything.

Only `percentile` does: the fraction it cuts at, `0.95` for a P95. `median` is the 0.5 one
and takes none. Every other measure refuses one rather than ignoring it, because a number
that is quietly dropped is a report that is quietly wrong.
argument.title: Argument

Measure.title: Measure

plus.description: How far to move it, signed: `{"days": -30}` is thirty days ago.

start_of.description: The start of the calendar unit it falls in once moved: `month` is the first of the month.

Offset.description:
Locating a page by counting rows from the start. **What everybody else does.**

    in      Offset(rows=160)                    the third page of eighty
    out     the rows after skipping 160

Here because an integration eventually counts pages, and because a strategy that exists is
better than one that gets bolted on. Honest about its cost: the database still walks the
skipped rows, and a row inserted mid-walk shifts everything after it — which is the bug
`Cursor` does not have.
Offset.title: Offset

Operator.description:
How a question is asked. **The enum's value is how it is written outside**, so the
definition publishes these same symbols in `ops` and no translation table exists anywhere.
Operator.title: Operator

Pagination.description:
How many, and from where.

    in      Pagination(limit=80)                              the first eighty
    in      Pagination(limit=80, strategy=Cursor(token="eyJ…"))   the next eighty
    in      Pagination(limit=80, strategy=Offset(rows=160))     the third page of eighty

Two separate things, and that is the point: **how many belongs to the page, from where is a
STRATEGY.** Cursor is one strategy and not the object — a caller that switches to counting
rows changes the strategy, not the way it asks for a page.

`limit` has a default and no ceiling. A framework says what happens when nobody chooses;
it does not decide for the application how much it may ask for.
Pagination.title: Pagination

Param.description: A value the caller supplied for this call: a typed text, a step's result.

name.description: The parameter, or a path into it with dots: `steps.order.total`.
name.title: Name

plus.description: How far to move it, signed: `{"days": -30}` is thirty days ago.

start_of.description: The start of the calendar unit it falls in once moved: `month` is the first of the month.

Param.title: Param

Part.description:
A number extracted from a date: the month of the year, whatever the year.

A grain **cuts** (a bucket is a range of time) and a part **extracts** (a bucket is a number
that many dates share), so they answer different questions: sales by month `2026-03` is a
grain, sales by «March, in any year» is a part. Weekdays count from Monday as 1, as ISO does.
Part.title: Part

Period.title: Period

Periods.description: A calendar span, as a closed range `[start, end)`. Only with the operator `between`.
Periods.title: Periods

Role.description: ``admin`` manages the tenant and approves; ``member`` asks for work.
Role.title: Role

Span.description:
A signed amount of time, by unit. Only the units asked for travel.

{"days": -30}                       thirty days back
{"months": 1, "days": -1}           a month ahead, a day back
Span.title: Span

Specification.description:
Field name → the criteria that says how to bring it.

    in      {"name": {}, "lines": {"pagination": {"limit": 20}}}
    out     Specification with two fields, the second carrying its own page

**One type and no union**: every value is a `Criteria`, the same one as outside, so a
consumer deserialises `dict[str, Criteria]` in any language and never has to tell a string
from an object. A scalar's is empty, because there is nothing to say about how to bring a
number. A relation's carries selection, order, pagination and its own specification, so the
vocabulary inside a node is the vocabulary outside it, at any depth.

A `RootModel` and not an object with one field inside: in JSON it is the bare mapping,
without a key that means nothing, and in here it has the methods that belong to it.
Specification.title: Specification

criteria.description:
Everything being asked: the filter, the ordering, the page and what to bring along.

One field rather than a parameter per filter, because a filter *is* a criteria — what the
interface calls a saved reading is the same object, merged.

cursor.description:
The `cursor` the previous answer came with, sent back as it is, to read the page after
it — none for the first page.
cursor.title: Cursor

drafts.description:
The caller's drafts instead of the stored records: filtered and ordered by the same
criteria, the most recently saved first when it names no order — one page, an owner's
drafts being few. What a client asks after it lost its state: what was I editing?
drafts.title: Drafts

count.description:
How many match in total, capped unless the criteria asked for the exact number.
`exact=False` means *at least* that many.

cursor.description: Where the next page starts. `None` means there is no next one.
cursor.title: Cursor

dropped.description:
Conditions the model could not answer — an unknown field, an operator its type does not
take. Reported rather than raised: a shared link outlives the schema it was written
against, and a dropped filter always widens the result.
dropped.title: Dropped

model_version.description:
The version of the model of the records — the fingerprint its published contract carries
(`x-sincpro.version`). What may be filtered, ordered and shown is described once, in the
discovery document; a client that holds another version loads the document again.
model_version.title: Model Version
